faculty.rank: Associate Professor; Faculty Fellowship #7 in Computer Science
faculty.research_areas: Rectified flow and ODE-based generative modelling; one-step generation via reflow/trajectory straightening; diffusion bridges and Doob's h-transform; optimal transport; variational and Monte Carlo inference; Stein methods; probabilistic graphical models
faculty.why_match: Akshat's DDPM-pretraining study on BTCV ran 500 epochs on a single NVIDIA A2000 and was expensive enough that he could not afford the ablations the result demanded: the frozen encoder retained roughly 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice (0.928 fine-tuned), but on kidney it scored 0.654, BELOW the 0.899 random-initialisation baseline, and he could never run the compute-matched SSL controls that would explain the split. Liu's 'Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow' straightens the ODE trajectories so that sampling collapses to a single Euler step — applying reflow on the pretraining side is a concrete route to making that per-organ ablation affordable rather than aspirational. Separately, Liu's framing of rectified flow as a transport map between two empirical distributions is a principled replacement for Akshat's A-PDF pipeline, where a cWGAN-GP is trained and then 66% of its 5,000 samples are thrown away by a post-hoc Mahalanobis filter because the discriminator could not be trusted.
faculty.key_paper_1: Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow — Xingchao Liu, Chengyue Gong, Qiang Liu; arXiv:2209.03003, 2022 (cited as [LGL22] on his official UT rectified-flow site)
faculty.key_paper_2: Let Us Build Bridges: Understanding and Extending Diffusion Generative Models — Xingchao Liu, Lemeng Wu, Mao Ye, Qiang Liu; arXiv:2208.14699, 2022

faculty.research_areas: Computer vision, machine learning, computer graphics; weakly and image-level supervised detection and segmentation; constrained output spaces; distillation from vision-language models; real-time and memory-efficient video/3D perception; autonomous driving perception
faculty.why_match: HiME's actual contribution is that hierarchy consistency is a property of the decoding rule rather than a measured number: per-level conditional sigmoids composed by the chain rule bound each child's probability by its parent's, so the prediction set is upward-closed by construction, at roughly 0.01% parameter overhead and with consistency 1.000 across all five backbones on Galaxy Zoo 2 (239,573 images, 37 classes, 4 levels). Krähenbühl's 'Constrained Convolutional Neural Networks for Weakly Supervised Segmentation' makes exactly that move — write the supervision as constraints on the output label distribution instead of relying on dense labels — and does it in Akshat's own modality, segmentation. His 'Detecting Twenty-thousand Classes using Image-level Supervision' is the label-efficiency counterpart to Akshat's SPIDER result, where a U-Net teacher trained on 54 labelled lumbar-spine images (0.735 mIoU) produced filtered pseudo-labels that lifted a student to 0.816 mIoU. Two of Akshat's ranked interests, A and C, meet inside one advisor's back catalogue, and F and G (real-time segmentation at 56 FPS on the autonomous go-kart) map onto his efficient-video line.

faculty.key_paper_2: Detecting Twenty-thousand Classes using Image-level Supervision — Xingyi Zhou, Rohit Girdhar, Armand Joulin, Philipp Krähenbühl, Ishan Misra; ECCV 2022

faculty.rank: Bettie Margaret Smith Professor of Engineering
faculty.department: Electrical and Computer Engineering AND Computer Science (joint)
faculty.lab: Director, NSF TRIPODS Institute at UT Austin; core member, NSF AI Institute for the Foundations of Machine Learning (IFML); Scientific Board, Center for Generative AI; member, Wireless Networking and Communications Group
faculty.research_areas: Theory and practice of large-scale model training; self-training and retraining with predicted labels; label noise; robust subset selection and data valuation; self-supervised learning theory; catastrophic forgetting and fine-tuning; mixtures of experts; diffusion language models
faculty.why_match: Akshat's SPIDER lumbar-spine study is an empirical instance of a theorem Sanghavi proved: a U-Net teacher trained on 54 labelled images reached 0.735 mIoU, and a student retrained on confidence-filtered pseudo-labels reached 0.816 mIoU (+8.1 absolute points), while unfiltered students stalled at 0.737-0.741. Sanghavi's 'Retraining with Predicted Hard Labels Provably Increases Model Accuracy' (ICML 2025) is exactly the analysis of why that retraining step gains, and would let Akshat convert his number into a mechanism. The second half of his portfolio hits the other open question in Akshat's work: 'Understanding Self-Supervised Learning via Gaussian Mixture Models' (NeurIPS 2025) speaks directly to why a frozen DDPM encoder kept ~87% of fine-tuned liver Dice but collapsed to 0.654 on kidney, below the 0.899 random-init baseline. His 'Geometric Median Matching for Robust k-Subset Selection from Noisy Data' also maps onto A-PDF's core move — selecting a trustworthy subset of generated samples by a distributional criterion instead of by discriminator score.

faculty.rank: Professor; Cockrell Family Chair in Engineering #15; Director, Center for Generative AI; IEEE Fellow
faculty.department: Electrical and Computer Engineering AND Computer Science (joint)
faculty.lab: Center for Generative AI (Director); Machine Learning Lab (MLL); Wireless Networking and Communications Group (WNCG)
faculty.research_areas: Diffusion models and generative AI; rectified differential equations and inversion/editing; statistical learning theory; what contrastive and in-context objectives provably learn; decision-making in wireless networks
faculty.why_match: Akshat's diffusion-pretraining result is unexplained in exactly the direction that matters: the frozen encoder kept roughly 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice but scored 0.654 on kidney, below the 0.899 random-init baseline, and 0.739 on multi-organ, below its 0.783 baseline. He therefore has hard evidence that a generative pretext task teaches something transferable for one structure and nothing for two others, and no account of why. Shakkottai's 'InfoNCE Loss Provably Learns Cluster-Preserving Representations' (COLT 2024) is precisely the genre of answer that is missing — a characterisation of what a self-supervised objective provably encodes about the data geometry — and pointing the same lens at the DDPM/score objective is a natural PhD problem. His 'Semantic Image Inversion and Editing using Stochastic Rectified Differential Equations' (ICLR 2025) connects to Akshat's A-PDF work, where a cWGAN-GP conditioned on orientation is followed by a Mahalanobis filter that keeps only 1,686 of 5,000 generated samples: a controllable rectified-flow inversion attacks the same problem without discarding two thirds of the compute.

faculty.key_paper_2: Semantic Image Inversion and Editing using Stochastic Rectified Differential Equations — ICLR 2025 (listed under 'Select Publications' on his UTCS faculty profile)

faculty.rank: Professor; Admiral B. R. Inman Centennial Chair in Computing Theory #2; Director of AI Initiatives, School of Computing
faculty.lab: Director, Machine Learning Lab (ml.utexas.edu); Director, IFML (NSF AI Institute for Foundations of Machine Learning); founder and co-director, UT Center for Generative AI; Director, Online Masters in AI (MSAI)
faculty.research_areas: Computational learning theory; testable learning and learning with distribution shift (TDS); learning under label noise, contamination and malicious noise; tester-learners; theory of diffusion/DDPM objectives; protein engineering with ML
faculty.why_match: Akshat's pseudo-label filtering sweep on SPIDER did not assume that confidence identifies correct pseudo-labels — it tested the assumption, and found per-class optimal thresholds raise pseudo-label IoU from 0.744 to 0.853, that Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty is merely comparable (0.791-0.792), and that combining the two adds nothing. Klivans' 'Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms' gives, in his own summary, 'the first efficient algorithms that can test if a training set satisfies the assumptions of a given noise model' — the formal version of the question Akshat answered empirically on a 54-image labelled set. Independently, 'Learning Mixtures of Gaussians using the DDPM Objective' shows that gradient descent on the score-estimation objective efficiently learns structure, which is the theoretical counterpart to Akshat's finding that DDPM pretraining yielded a transferable frozen encoder for liver but one that fell below random initialisation for kidney.
faculty.key_paper_1: Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms — Surbhi Goel, Adam Klivans, Kostas Stavropoulos, Arsen Vasilyan; to appear COLT 2026 (arXiv:2501.09189). Best Paper Award, NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Reliable ML.
faculty.key_paper_2: Learning Mixtures of Gaussians using the DDPM Objective — Kulin Shah, Sitan Chen, Adam Klivans; NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2307.01178)
faculty.taking_students: Unstated — no recruiting statement. Group is currently three PhD students (Kostas Stavropoulos, Gautam Chandrasekaran, Kulin Shah), two postdocs (Vasilis Kontonis, Arsen Vasilyan) and one research scientist (Danny Diaz), which is a small and highly selective theory group.
faculty.email_angle: I swept confidence thresholds against Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty for filtering pseudo-labels and found that combining them adds nothing — your 'Testing Noise Assumptions' paper is the principled version of the check I was running by hand, and I would like to understand what it would say about my setting.
faculty.notes: CONFIRMED at UT Austin — the tracker's duplicate CMU listing is wrong; delete it. Classified PARTIAL rather than Close on METHOD fit, not topic fit: his output is COLT/STOC/FOCS/NeurIPS-theory (TDS learning, tester-learners, robustly learning halfspaces, learning juntas under MRFs), and Akshat has zero theory output and describes himself as a rigorous empiricist. Naming Klivans as an intended primary advisor in the SOP would invite the question 'where is your theory?'. He is nevertheless the most strategically important person on this list because he simultaneously runs the ML Lab, IFML and the Center for Generative AI — worth one respectful sentence in the SOP as institutional context, not as the advisor ask. He also runs an applied protein-engineering line with research scientist Danny Diaz (e.g. 'Predicting a Protein's Stability under a Million Mutations', NeurIPS 2023, jointly with Krähenbühl) which is the empirical door into his orbit. Awards: FOCS Test of Time (2025), COLT Best Paper (2024).

faculty.lab: Zhou research group (probabilistic machine learning / generative AI)
faculty.research_areas: Probabilistic machine learning and Bayesian analysis; diffusion distillation and one-step generation (SiD / SiD-LSG); diffusion-GAN hybrids; patch and beta diffusion; approximate inference; RL and preference optimisation for LLMs
faculty.why_match: Score identity Distillation is the closest thing on the UT Austin campus to a direct answer to Akshat's binding constraint: his DDPM pretraining on BTCV ran 500 epochs on a single NVIDIA A2000 and still left the decisive ablation unaffordable, so the finding that a frozen encoder retained ~87% of fine-tuned liver Dice while scoring 0.654 on kidney (below the 0.899 random-init baseline) remains an observation rather than an explanation. Zhou's 'Diffusion-GAN: Training GANs with Diffusion' is also a pointed counterpoint to A-PDF: Akshat explicitly refused to trust his cWGAN-GP discriminator and instead scored generated masks against the class-proportion distribution of 447 real masks, with Mahalanobis retaining only 1,686 of 5,000 samples — Diffusion-GAN makes the opposite bet, repairing the discriminator itself by feeding it diffusion-noised inputs. That is a genuine disagreement worth a paragraph.

faculty.key_paper_2: Patch Diffusion — NeurIPS 2023 (listed in the 09/2023 news entry on his official site)

I am currently working full time at Microsoft AI while maintaining my faculty position at UT Austin.' faculty.rank: Associate Professor; William J. Murray, Jr. Fellowship in Engineering
faculty.department: Chandra Family Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, with appointments in the Department of Diagnostic Medicine (Dell Medical School) and the Oden Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences. NO Computer Science appointment listed.
faculty.lab: Computational Sensing and Imaging (CSI) Lab — github.com/utcsilab
faculty.research_areas: Computational magnetic resonance imaging; diffusion and score-based generative priors for inverse problems; learning from corrupted/noisy data; memory-efficient learning for large-scale imaging; unsupervised reconstruction without ground truth; benchmark integrity in medical imaging ML; pediatric MRI translation
faculty.why_match: Akshat's method identity is 'test the assumption nobody tested', and Tamir wrote the canonical paper in that genre for medical imaging: 'Implicit data crimes: Machine learning bias arising from misuse of public data' (PNAS 2022) shows how preprocessing choices on public datasets silently inflate reported performance. That is precisely the failure mode Akshat found inside his own polyp work, where the headline three-class average Dice of 0.9525 is not comparable to binary polyp-only baselines and the recoverable polyp-only Dice of ~0.873 actually sits below three of four comparators. Second, Tamir's 'Ambient Diffusion Posterior Sampling: Solving Inverse Problems with Diffusion Models Trained on Corrupted Data' attacks from the training side the exact problem A-PDF attacks from the filtering side: Akshat built a Mahalanobis/kNN filter over the class-proportion distribution of 447 real masks because he could not trust generated data, whereas Tamir asks how to learn a usable generative prior when the data itself is not clean.
faculty.key_paper_1: Implicit data crimes: Machine learning bias arising from misuse of public data — E. Shimron, J. I. Tamir, K. Wang, M. Lustig; Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2022;119(13):e2117203119
faculty.key_paper_2: Ambient Diffusion Posterior Sampling: Solving Inverse Problems with Diffusion Models Trained on Corrupted Data — A. Aali, G. Daras, B. Levac, S. Kumar, A. G. Dimakis, J. I. Tamir; arXiv:2403.08728, March 2024
faculty.taking_students: Unstated — no recruiting statement on his homepage or CSI Lab page as of 2026-08-28.
faculty.email_angle: I found that my own polyp segmentation paper's headline margin evaporates once you separate the trivially separable third class from the actual polyp Dice — 'Implicit data crimes' is the paper that named the disease I diagnosed in my own work, and I want to do research where that check is the starting point rather than the afterthought.

faculty.research_areas: Computer vision, computer graphics and machine learning; 3D generative models that enforce geometric, physical and topological priors; learning from limited 3D data; consistency constraints across map networks; statistical data analysis, compressive sensing, low-rank matrix recovery, large-scale optimization
faculty.why_match: HiME's real contribution is that hierarchy consistency is a theorem of the decoding rule rather than a measured statistic — chain-rule composition bounds each child's probability by its parent's, giving an upward-closed prediction set with consistency 1.000 across all five tested backbones. Huang's 'Path-Invariant Map Networks' (CVPR 2019, oral, Best Paper Finalist) is the same manoeuvre transplanted to geometry: enforce consistency across a network of maps as a structural property rather than a soft penalty. And his current agenda, verbatim from his own homepage, is 'developing 3D generative models that enforce geometric, physical, and topological priors and learn from both 3D and 2D that address issues of limited 3D data and generalization' — which is Akshat's interests C and B compressed into one sentence, including the limited-data framing that motivates all of his own work.
